I came across intel's (archived) TAA (licensed under MIT) this morning which helped to clarify some of the things I was uncertain about and made me realize that there are a couple of things I could do better. Will mark this as draft for now while I am experimenting. My current local version has already changed significantly (re-added dynamic box size, made the entire TAA operate in reinhard, added kari weight to clipping for anti flicker) EDIT: Here are some new images of the changes I just pushed. The first commit re-added the dynamic box size (but using math more in line with what intel is doing), made sure TAA operated entirely in reinhard and finally added luminance based weights to the neighbourhood samples to try and remove fireflies.
Commit 1
The second commit is a bit bigger. It adds two additional buffers to TAA, which are used to track the current accumulation count for every pixel. This makes it possible to dynamically the change the weights, which should hopefully result in a more stable image. As a consequence I also adjusted the reset logic a bit, though I plan to tweak that further in the future.
new accum buffers
The changes are subtle, but the checkerboard floor is now a bit more accurate, and the ear of the fox now looks significantly better. You can also notice subtle changes when you look at the right side of the helmet, when new pixels are disoccluded.

Ok, pushed a handful more changes. In order I did:

### Blend in the surrounding pixels after disocclusion
```
	// On reset we will fall back to color_input, which is a single aliased sample
	// If a reset is happening blend in an average of the neighborhood to avoid shimmer & aliasing
	color_input = mix(color_input, fallback_neighborhood_avg(pos_group), reset_factor * 0.5);
```

### Adjusted the neighborhood shape
Multiple of my references mentioned that for the neighborhood shape they combined a 3x3 bos with 5 taps in a plus shape.
I implemented that with an array of weights.

### Don't dilate the velocity on the sky
When moving the camera in the editor I had problems with the edges between meshes and the skybox. A simple depth check mitigated that.

### Replace the clip_aabb function
I found the current clip_aabb function somewhat questionable. In the end I replaced it with the [slab method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slab_method). This resulted in slight visual differences (improvements imo). Given that the slab method is the widely accepted state of the art and the fact that all my test scenes looked either identical or better I decided to go with it.

---

I also added one more photo of the test scene I already showed before in the inital post. Left the commits unsquashed for now to make it easier to review.

Would appreciate it if people could test this with their own project and report back. I personally think this is a big step forward, but my testing was limited to a mere handful of projects, could very well be that there are edge cases I missed.
Seems to be working fine. Just a minor flickering with SSR but I guess its inevitable
Could you please optimize TAA as much as possible? This has also been raised as an issue.

> Could you please optimize TAA as much as possible? This has also been raised as an issue.

The goal was to keep this as simple as possible to hopefully get it merged quickly. This was meant to be a small side project while my meshlet work was stuck.

The obvious performance wins would be to use more ping-ponging (which would probably require me to change buffer logic throughout the renderer) and to do something about the catmull rom (which has 9 taps), but which I hesitated to touch due to quality concerns.

I was happy enough that my changes didn't result into a noticeable performance loss and was planning to leave it there, but I guess I have an hour or two to kill this evening. Please don't expect any miracles.

Ok, did a performance pass. Nothin really major, but managed to eliminate a couple unnecessary buffer copies and removed four taps from the catmull rom.

As far as I am concerned this is done now. There is not really anything left to change tbh. Will leave the commits unsquashed for now in case the rendering team wants me to revert some of the changes.

According to nsight I got the performance from `~0.49ms` to `~0.38ms` on my 5080 when doing TAA for a 4k frame.

<details>
<summary>Detailed list of the performance related changes I made today:</summary>

## TAA Baseline 4k
```
Resolve TAA 					0.34ms, samples from nsight flamegraph
	- main (due to barrier) 	25.25%
	- populate_group_shared		18.97%
		- long scoreboard		40%
		- memory barrier		36%
	- catmull rom				14.95%
	- to ycoc + from ycocg		4.23% + 0.16%
Resolve Pipeline Barrier 		<0.01ms

Copy tmp -> internal			0.07ms
Copy Velocity					0.07ms

Pipeline Barrier      			<0.01ms

Copy History					0.07ms
	- this copies from internal and not tmp, resulting in an otherwise unnecessary barrier
	- could be removed entirely with ping pong

Pipeline Barrier				<0.01ms
```
## TAA PingPong Output 4k
```
Resolve TAA						0.34ms
Resolve Pipeline Barrier 		<0.01ms

Copy output -> internal			0.07ms
Copy Velocity					0.07ms

Pipeline Barrier      			<0.01ms
```
## TAA Velocity nonsense

Tried having the resovle shader output this frames velocity to next frame's history buffer. My hope was that the imageLoad in `getClosestPixelVelocity` would often enough end up picking this pixels velocity that a second load immediately after it would almost always hit the cache and be essentially free.

It did not work out that way in practice (slower by 0.02ms onm average).

## TAA Velocity 2

Have the resolve pass write the dilated velocity into the history buffer instead. Slight visual change, but we can still eliminate an entire copy.

```
Resolve TAA						0.37ms
Resolve Pipeline Barrier 		<0.01ms

Copy output -> internal			0.07ms

Pipeline Barrier      			<0.01ms
```

## 5 tap Catmull Rom

This slightly lowers the image quality, but the difference is barely noticeable without a subtract view.
```
Resolve TAA						0.32ms
Resolve Pipeline Barrier 		<0.01ms

Copy output -> internal			0.07ms

Pipeline Barrier      			<0.01ms
```

## Populate group combine depth and color into one vec4
```
Resolve TAA						0.30ms
Resolve Pipeline Barrier 		<0.01ms

Copy output -> internal			0.07ms

Pipeline Barrier      			<0.01ms
```

While working on this I also noticed a fun bug. load_color and load_depth accepted uvec2 and then added 1 to it. Without relying on wraparound this would have made it impossible to access index 0 in the shared data.
While the current code technically worked due to wraparound I switched it over to ivec2 to be more explicit.

I also packed the accum count into the alpha channel of the history buffer.

</details>

I also just updated the screenshots in the first post. There are some minor visual degradations as a result of my performance improvements, but unless you are comnparing them side by side with a subtract shader I don't think anyone will notice them.

As before, if you have a project using TAA I would be happy to receive any feedback. I myself tested this change in only 5 projects, and 4 of them were tiny demo projects. Would love to see how this performs in a real game.

EDIT: also would like performance numbers on other hardware. My 5080 is probably not representative of what the typical player is using.

Oh god, I found it. This was a nightmare btw.

As it turns the shimmer was caused by the new slab AABB in combination with the switch to YCoCg. For those that don't know, YCoCg encode luma into Y, and chroma into Co and Cg.
However, for anything that is grey this means that `Co = Cg = 0`. When we feed this into the slab method we end up with `tMax.co = 0` and `direction.co = 0`, which results in `tFar` also becoming 0. The final return value is thus the average color with the history being discarded.

Tbh the only reason I managed to figure this out is because this problem wasn't visible in any of my own test scenes. I was more interested in scenes with complicated geometry and movements and thus never tried a scene that contained a true grey surface.
When I finally compared unshaded output of your scene to my scenes I realized that the shimmering surfaces all had no chromacity, at which point the problem became obvious.

Will push a fix later today.

EDIT: amended the original use slab commit to contain my fix.
The issue has already been resolved, thank you.

Several comments
1) Tonemapping should be skipped, it causes issues with thin Bright objects like bullets or street lamps dimming their glow and also completely wrecking Tonemapper results (causing ACES and AGX to give very saturated results incorrectly)
DLSS 4 (or 4.5 don't remember) ditched the internal Tonemapping step for similar reasons a while back
2) Edges of objects are still subject to the pixel thick expansion-contraction issue to a degree
3) Depth in closest velocity is nonsensical. Min depth is 1.0, and the depth range is 0-1, and the check `depth>min_depth` always returns false because the depth is never going to be greater then 1 (only equal if the object is right in the camera's face, so in practice not really ever)
Min Depth should be renamed to Closest Depth and should start at 0 instead of 1

Added some more minor tweaks and rebased on master

> 1. Tonemapping should be skipped

The internal reinhard tonemapping is completely reversed before the output is written. In my personal tests it hasn't had a negative impact on the final grade or any emissive surfaces. If you perform TAA directly in linear HDR a single bright firefly can completely skew the output result, resulting in aliasing. Some kind of internal tonemapping is needed, but if you have an alternative suggestion I am eager to hear it.

You can also build this PR locally and replace the `reinhard` and `reinhard_inverse` functions with stubs to test this. (And send any screenshots you take, I am always eager to have more data).

> 2. Too much dilation

I added a dilation limit that should help mitigate that a bit. However, there is not much more I can do about this, to properly alias edges I need to dilate the velocity buffer at least a bit.

> 3. Depth in closest_velocity

Yep, that function was badly broken when reverse depth was merged a while ago. Good catch. Fun fact, there is another completely unrelated bug in the original `get_closest_pixel_velocity_3x3` function: when sampling velocity it uses `group_top_left + min_pos`. However, `group_top_left` also includes `- kBorderSize`, so all the velocities this function returned where for a pixel with an offset with `(-1, -1)`.

That bug has been fixed in my PR as well, but after some testing I switched from using depth for velocity dilation to using magnitude. In some of my test scenes that helped me anti alias some edges that depth based dilation didn't catch.
For now I left the original  dilation code in the shader and only commented it out. Might give it another try in the future, but so far I am liking the results I get with magnitude based dilation

I think I will leave things here for now (unless someone finds another bug). I still have some more ideas that can be implemented to improve things (e.g. supplying an alpha mask, unjittering the textures, ...) but this PR has already ballooned way beyond my plans.

Tested latest branch Edge problems are significantly reduced, and the overall quality and stability is now a massive improvement. The Tonemapping isn't required when you've got a 5 tap avg for reset as that handles the fireflies fairly well. Now granted in most scenarios it isn't awful but take this as an example caused by the internal tonemap TAA with tonemap SMAA FSR 2.2 Native

If you send me that scene (or just a tiny reproduction project showing the same problem) I can play around with the current shader and try to get it looking more like SMAA, without loosing quality in my other testscenes.

The thing is that without reinhard specular highlights can become a real problem and poison the surrounding pixels, but maybe the other anti flicker I already have will be enough.

The Edge Contraction and Expansion problems are resolved if you move from magnitude to the fixed closest depth. Also Magnitude Dilation is a really bad idea, as it results in poor consistency of edge picks. Take this kind of an example. Background motion vectors are going in one direction, but the Foreground object motion vectors are going in another, both with similar magnitudes, which is it going to pick? Who knows... Also yeah ok I have found instances where removing the internal Tonemapping does hurt stability quite a bit, so maybe not a good idea to remove it right now. Additionally, just an idea, why not relax history rejection the lower the depth value (aka further away from the camera)? Just as a side Note, I tested this on Nvidia's RTX branch, and it's doing a fantastic job at handling the noise (considering no Denoiser is available for AMD rn) and is doing far better compared to FSR 2 and old TAA and any of my own attempts Likely for future PR, I think with TAA gizmos should be made to be non transparent

> unjittering the textures

I recall something like this being discovered by [Luma](https://github.com/Filoppi/Luma-Framework) modders in at least one game (I think Mafia 2 or 3?) and it was frowned upon, because it effectively canceled the specular antialiasing benefits of TAA. But yes, it's technically possible by shifting UV coordinates to cancel out the per-vertex jitter.

> Likely for future PR, I think with TAA gizmos should be made to be non transparent

Gizmos are already using alpha scissor transparency, which means they write to the depth buffer. (This is also what makes them appear in SSAO and SSR, although ideally we'd probably want to prevent that without introducing transparency sorting issues.)
since after 4.7.2? that's what I'm using with this modded in

Ok I have an idea how to solve the glow issue.

The Glow has to happen on a non-antialiased buffer that is just de-jittered

Alternatively the hack I'm using is removing Reinhard and applying the Reinhard exclusively to luminance (not the hacky part) and checking if the current pixel without AA has a length of 100 or more and if so I just set it as resolve instead of applying AA (aka the hacky part) which results in glowing things looking very similar to MSAA, just slightly flickery, probably because no de-jittering is taking place.

> since after 4.7.2? that's what I'm using with this modded in

Since 4.3:

- https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/91174
Well, if so gizmos are not writing any motion vectors

> Gizmos are already using alpha scissor transparency, which means they write to the depth buffer. [...]

Uhh, Nsight would disagree with you on that point. Can't see the axis or the grid in neither the depth nor the velocity buffer.
* node_3d_editor_plugin.cpp:1094 `render_mode blend_mix`
* node_3d_editor_plugin.cpp:1220 writes to alpha in fragment

It would be trivial to kick them into the opaque pass, but that is a decision I will leave to someone with more editor UX experience.

The alternative would be to wait for some general transparency improvements for TAA. Right now I have the following (very vague) idea:
	1. subtract pre alpha frame from post alpha frame, store normalized result in an alpha_diff buffer
	2. In TAA load the alpha_diff texture and compare it to prev_alpha_diff, use result to reset accumulation when alpha has major changes
	
There are probably better ways to do this, this is just the first option I can think of that won't require us to write to some stencil buffer whenever we are rendering alpha materials.

Either way, this is something beyond the scope of this PR, given how poor the current implementation is at handling alpha.

> The Edge Contraction and Expansion problems are resolved if you move from magnitude to the fixed closest depth.

The reason I am using magnitude is because it does a far better job at detecting edges where two objects intersect. With depth both pixels have near identical depth, which can result in taa not picking up the edge properly.
Two objects moving in opposite direction with the exact same velocity (relative to the camera) is faaaar less likely to happen.
If you check the intel implementation you can see that they are also using magnitude.

In my test scenes I have seen no example where magnitude has resulted in a noticeably worse image, while the opposite wasn't true. But I would be happy to change it back if you have an example that proves me wrong.

> Also yeah ok I have found instances where removing the internal Tonemapping does hurt stability quite a bit

Yeah. I am not entirely happy with this. I considered using some kind of tonemapping function that has a saddlepoint. That might allow us to compress specular fireflies, while keeping intentionally bright and emissive pixels. However, I fear that any such implementation would have to be very scene dependant.
If you have some time that might be something worth exploring for a follow up PR.

I believe Unreal has solved this by exposing a "control"-texture. If devs have bright materials they want to preserve they write a bit to this texture. TAA reads from this texture and then gives additional weight to this pixel. (Somewhat similar to my proposed alpha texture).

---

I can't really think of any more easy wins that are generally applicable for TAA, without optimizing it for a certain usecase. Especially given that I want to keep TAA as cheap as possible, since on more powerful systems it oftentimes makes more sense to use an upscaler for AA instead anyways.

Is there any further feedback I should try to work on this weekend? Given that the feature freeze has begun I will otherwise shift my focus back to meshlet rendering, in hopes of having a proof of concept PR ready for the next dev cycle.
